name: Kryždirbystė Cross
description: Carved oak wayside crosses of the Lithuanian cross-crafting tradition, one to five metres tall, with small roofs, carved figures and flower and geometric ornament, standing at village entrances, crossroads, cemeteries and shrines. Once consecrated by a priest, a cross is sacred and draws offerings — food, rosaries, scarves and aprons — seeking fertility, healing or protection, and the craft's masters, the kryždirbiai, shape stogastulpiai, koplytstulpiai and full crosses in styles that vary from region to region. Under Russian imperial rule and again under the Soviet occupation the wayside cross became a symbol of national identity, and in 2001 the tradition was proclaimed by UNESCO a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Cross-crafting and its symbolism (2001); LNKC Savadas (Lithuanian National Culture Centre)

name: Lietuviška Juosta
description: Hand-woven sash of linen and wool, rich with geometric patterns in several colours, worn by Lithuanian men and women wrapped at the waist over festive dress and given as gifts at weddings, christenings and funerals. The juosta was woven on narrow looms or by tablet weaving, and every region knew its own ornament — rhombuses, zigzags, crosses and small stars — so that a sash could name the wearer's parish. In folk belief the sash was protective: it binds, fastens and marks a sacred boundary, and a woven band given away could carry goodwill or serve as an offering, mediating between people and the spirits of field and forest.
source: Ethnographic studies of Lithuanian sash symbolism (Lietuvių juostų simbolika, Lituanistika)

name: Verbos Easter Palms
description: Tall bouquets of dried and dyed grasses, flowers, mosses, juniper and willow, bound with leaves and seeds onto a rod of hazel or willow, carried to church on Palm Sunday for consecration and kept afterwards in an honoured place at home. The verba tradition has been practised for at least seven generations in villages northwest of Vilnius and is documented in paintings and ethnographies since the mid-1800s, and the palms are still made for Palm Sunday, for Easter and for the St. Casimir's Fair in Vilnius each March. The consecrated verba is kept by the household as a protection against storms and misfortune, hung behind the door or on the wall through the year.
material: dried and dyed grasses, flowers, juniper, willow, hazel rod
source: LNKC Savadas: The tradition of tying verbos (Easter palms) in Vilnius region; documentary records since Kanutas Ruseckas (1847) and Oscar Kolberg (1866)

name: Kanklės
description: Archaic Lithuanian plucked box zither, a trapezoid of solid wood — maple, linden or ash — hollowed from a single piece and strung with parallel strings, of the same Baltic psaltery family as the Latvian kokle and the Estonian kannel. Old belief held that the bards, the vaidilos, sang heroic songs and served the gods to its music, and that the best instrument wood was cut between a person's death and funeral, for a mourned tree lent the kanklės a sorrowful, spirit-voiced tone. The instrument accompanied wedding songs and dances, its players, the kanklininkai, being honoured guests, and it was revived in the twentieth-century folk revival as a national instrument.
material: maple, linden or ash wood, wire or gut strings
source: LNKC survey of Lithuanian string instruments (chordophones); Lithuanian ethnomusicology

name: Eglė's Dress
description: In the Lithuanian tale 'Eglė the Queen of Serpents', the garment Eglė wore when she bathed at the lake: a coiled grass snake slipped into her sleeve and would return her clothing only if she promised to marry its king. That pledged dress drives the whole tale — the serpent bridegroom, nine years lived beneath the sea, three impossible tasks set for her children — and at the end Eglė, refusing to follow her transformed husband's cruelty, is changed into a spruce tree, while her children become the oak, ash and birch of the Lithuanian forest. The dress is the object that binds the human and the serpent world in one of the best-loved tales of the Baltic.
source: Lithuanian folk tale 'Eglė žalčių karalienė'; first translation printed 1837 by M. Jasevičius, recorded in Lithuanian folklore collections

name: Lielvārde Belt
description: The Lielvārde belt: a wide woven wool sash of red-and-white geometric patterns, with small figures worked into the bands, worn with Latvian folk costume and woven in the Lielvārde region of central Latvia. Folklore remembers it as a protective band that warded off evil, and since the 1970s the repeating patterns have been read by some as a hidden code of the universe — even of human DNA — a theory championed in popular writing though not by all scholars. The folklorist Janīna Kursīte traces its red-white symbolism to ancient protective clothing and incantations, and the belt was admitted to the Latvian Cultural Canon in 2008 as a national symbol.
maker: Latvian village weavers of the Lielvārde region
source: Latvijas Kultūras kanons: Lielvārdas josta (2008); folklore researcher Janīna Kursīte

name: Sakta Brooch
description: The sakta, the ancient Baltic breast brooch of bronze, silver or silver-gilt, fastened the folk costume — above all the bride's — at throat or chest, in one or several at once. Archaeological finds date the fibula type back roughly two millennia, and the later 'bubble' saktas, with hemispherical bosses set with glass studs, were trusted as a woman's savings, pinned to her dress as a portable store of value. A Latvian folk song says the goddess Laima makes fibulae for a girl, 'immersing them in silver', and the brooch was given at the coming-of-age ceremonies of girls and kept as an heirloom of the family.
source: Latvijas Banka, Gold Brooches: The Bubble Fibula; Latvian archaeological and ethnographic collections

name: Kokle
description: The Latvian plucked box zither: a trapezoid soundbox with parallel strings over a flat board, carved from maple, ash or lime, played by strumming and plucking. A chronicle entry of 1225, when Henricus de Lettis wrote of a kokle played by Livonian youths, makes it the oldest documented psaltery in Europe, and Latvian folk songs call its strings 'silver war' and 'golden war'. The kokle accompanied the dainas, the great corpus of Latvian folksong, and in the twentieth century a larger concert kokle was developed; in 2008 the kokle and the art of koklēšana were placed in the Latvian Cultural Canon as the national instrument.
material: maple or ash wood, metal strings
source: Latvijas Kultūras kanons: Kokles un koklēšana (2008); Henricus de Lettis (1225)

name: Laima's Distaff
description: The distaff of fate in Latvian and Lithuanian belief: a carved spindle-holder on which the goddess Laima, or the forest fairy Lauma, spins and measures the thread of a human life, fixing its length and its luck. Folk accounts describe laumas borrowing distaffs and spindles from village women and spinning linen by night, and the spindle's turning thread stands in countless spinning dainas for fate being spun out for a newborn child. The distaff itself was a treasured, often carved and painted object passed from mother to daughter, so that the homely tool of flax-spinning carried a double meaning: the thread of cloth and the thread of destiny.
source: Latvian and Lithuanian folklore accounts of Laima and laumas as spinners of fate (Latvian dainas; Britannica: Laima)

name: Jāņi Wreath
description: The midsummer wreath of Jāņi: for women and girls, plaited from flowers, grasses, herbs and leaves, a braid of twenty-seven plants being held to ward off disasters, disease and enemies, while men and boys wore rings of oak leaves as tokens of strength. Worn through Līgo night on 23 June with singing, cheese, beer and bonfire jumping, the wreath is kept afterwards — hung in the house, given to the cattle or laid under the pillow — for protection and healing through the year. The customs, described since the seventeenth century, make the wreath the visible emblem of the great festival of the Latvian summer solstice.
source: Latvian Jāņi folklore; midsummer customs documented since Paul Einhorn (1627)

name: Estonian Kannel
description: Estonia's plucked box zither, a small winged or trapezoid instrument carved from a single piece of wood and strung with wire or gut strings, played to accompany regilaul, the ancient runic-song tradition shared with Finland's kantele and Lithuania's kanklės. Folk songs and folk archaeology place the kannel in Baltic-Finnic music for well over a thousand years, and the instrument was long the companion of song and dance in the village. It survives and flourishes in the folk revival, where ensembles play both the small historical kannel and enlarged chromatic versions, keeping the oldest instrument of Estonian music on the concert stage.
material: carved wood, wire or gut strings
source: Estonian folk music scholarship; Estonian National Museum instrument collections

name: Seto Folk Costume
description: The Seto women's folk costume of south-eastern Estonia's Setomaa: a striking white, black and red ensemble of striped or checked skirt, linen blouse, woven belt and heavy silver jewellery, above all the large seto silver brooch with its coin pendants. The costume is integral to leelo, the polyphonic singing tradition inscribed by UNESCO in 2009, for the Seto choir sang in traditional dress, and it is worn for church feasts, weddings and Seto Kingdom Day, where it announces the wearer's village and lineage. The dress is made and passed down by Seto women, whose handicraft knowledge — of weaving, embroidery and silverwork — is as much a part of Setomaa's heritage as its songs.
source: UNESCO: Seto Leelo, Seto polyphonic singing tradition (2009); Visit Setomaa ethnographic accounts

name: Kihnu Woolen Skirt
description: The striped woolen skirt and knitted garments of Kihnu Island's women: bright red, green and blue striped cloth woven on home looms from local wool, worn with embroidered blouses, sashes, mittens and stockings whose colours and patterns recall old legends. With the island's men long at sea, Kihnu's women carried the culture of the island, and the making of these garments — together with the songs, dances and handicraft skills of the Kihnu cultural space inscribed by UNESCO in 2003 — became an emblem of Estonian island identity. The striped skirt, folded and held by a woven belt, is still worn daily by older women and with pride at festivals.
source: UNESCO: Kihnu cultural space (2003); Kihnu women's handicraft tradition

name: Kirivöö Belt
description: The kirivöö, the Estonian pick-up patterned belt: a narrow woven band of wool over a linen or wool ground, carrying rows of small crosses, rhombuses, triangles and diagonal figures worked by the pick-up technique. Each parish knew its own edge patterns, so that the belt could tell where a woman came from, and the belts were worn wrapped at the waist with folk dress, and given as gifts, love-pledges and protective charms. The Estonian National Museum holds belts from across the country, and studies of the small patterns at the belt edges continue to map the regional styles and their meanings.
source: Studia Vernacula: 'Small patterns at the edges of belts' (Estonian National Museum, 2018)

name: Põhjanael
description: The Põhjanael, the 'North Nail', the Estonian folk name for the North Star: in the old Baltic-Finnic worldview the sky was an upturned cauldron or great wheel turning on a nail driven through its centre, and that nail is Polaris. Farmers read the seasons from the stars turning around it, and folk sayings spoke of the sky-wheel's spokes and of the nail that holds the heavens fixed. The folklorist Matthias Johann Eisen recorded the motif in his 'Eesti Mütoloogia' and folk-astronomy notes, preserving a sky-picture in which the fixed North Star is the axle of the whole turning world.
source: M. J. Eisen, Eesti Mütoloogia IV; Estonian folk astronomy tradition

name: Latvian Josta (Woven Belt)
description: Ornamental belt woven by Latvian women on a small rigid loom, patterned with geometric symbols of the sun, moon and stars and the zigzag josta motif, worn by men to hold shirt and breeches. A full-length josta measures several metres and is wound twice around the waist; its weaving is a living craft, and the Latvian National Centre for Culture keeps a register of master weavers. The belt is part of the national costume worn at song festivals, and its symbols are read as protective signs: the sun for light, the grass snake for the household, and the endless repeating band for continuity. Traditionally the josta was a woman's gift, woven for her husband or son, and a richly patterned belt showed both the weaver's skill and the family's standing. Museum examples from the 19th century show the standard red, white and green palette with the black zigzag that gives the belt its name.
source: Latvian National Centre for Culture (josta pattern register)
